scenes.tts: Language is left-dominant in most people. Yet in one study of 326 healthy adults, right-hemisphere dominance appeared in about one strong left-hander in four. Does that make most left-handers right-dominant? It does not. To see why, we need the base rate.

scenes.narration: Language is left-dominant in most people. Yet in one study of 326 healthy adults, right-hemisphere dominance appeared in about 1 strong left-hander in 4. Does that make most left-handers right-dominant? It does not. To see why, we need the base rate.

scenes.tts: How was dominance measured? With ultrasound over each temple, while people generated words. This is called functional transcranial Doppler. The side whose blood flow rises more is scored as dominant. Right-hemisphere dominance appeared in four percent of strong right-handers, fifteen percent of ambidextrous people, and twenty-seven percent of strong left-handers. Left-handedness raises the odds of right-sided language. It does not make it typical.

scenes.tts: Now an exercise. Use the study's rates as fixed probabilities. Think of each person as one dot, blue for right-handers and yellow for left-handers. Take one hundred strong right-handers and one hundred strong left-handers. These group sizes are assumptions, not measured. Expect four of the right-handers to be right-dominant, and twenty-seven of the left-handers. That makes thirty-one right-dominant people in all.

scenes.tts: Now pick one right-dominant person at random. This question runs backward from the one we started with. How likely is it that this person is left-handed? Twenty-seven of the thirty-one are. That is eighty-seven percent. Yet only twenty-seven percent of left-handers are right-dominant. These are two different questions.
scenes.caption: Now pick one right-dominant person at random. This question runs backward from the one we started with. How likely is it that this person is left-handed? 27 of the 31 are. That is 87%. Yet only 27% of left-handers are right-dominant. These are two different questions.

scenes.narration: Now pick one right-dominant person at random. This question runs backward from the one we started with. How likely is it that this person is left-handed? 27 of the 31 are. That is 87%. Yet only 27% of left-handers are right-dominant. These are two different questions.

scenes.tts: Now change only the population. Make it ninety percent strong right-handers and ten percent strong left-handers. The rates stay the same. Each group contributes its share of the population times its rate. Right-handers contribute point zero three six. Left-handers contribute point zero two seven. Together, right-dominant people are six point three percent of the population.
scenes.caption: Now change only the population. Make it 90% strong right-handers and 10% strong left-handers. The rates stay the same. Each group contributes its share of the population times its rate. Right-handers contribute 0.036. Left-handers contribute 0.027. Together, right-dominant people are 6.3% of the population.

scenes.narration: Now change only the population. Make it 90% strong right-handers and 10% strong left-handers. The rates stay the same. Each group contributes its share of the population times its rate. Right-handers contribute 0.036. Left-handers contribute 0.027. Together, right-dominant people are 6.3% of the population.

scenes.tts: Pick a right-dominant person again. The chance of being left-handed is now point zero two seven over point zero six three. That is forty-three percent. The rates did not change. The base rate did, and the answer fell from eighty-seven to forty-three percent. Right-sided language is now more often found in a right-hander, simply because right-handers are so many. Left-handedness shifts the odds of right-sided language without reversing them. Same rates, different base rate, different answer.
